a: some of the scribes who had arrived from Jerusalem
p: This is the second visit by scribes from Jerusalem in Mark. The first group said Jesus had Beelzebul.
b: Scribes "who came down from Jerusalem" already accused Jesus of working with the ruler of the demons (3:22). Mark's readers are meant to remember them: opposition is now coming from the religious capital, where Jesus will die (10:33). The Pharisees were a lay movement within Judaism that kept purity and tithing with special care; scribes were experts in the law of Moses, some of them Pharisees. The debate that follows is a debate among Jews about how to keep God's law. Jesus answers it as a Jewish teacher, from the Torah and the Prophets.

p: Mark's word is koinos, "common": not dirty, but not set apart for holy use. He explains it for readers who did not know.
b: Koinos means "common, shared." In Jewish Greek it came to mean ritually impure, the opposite of holy (1 Maccabees 1:47, 62; Acts 10:14). The disciples' hands are not filthy; they have not been through the rinsing that some Jews used to keep ordinary food pure. Mark adds "which means unwashed hands" because his readers would not know the term. He uses a different word, akathartos, for "unclean" spirits (7:25). The Plain keeps "common," as in Peter's vision (Acts 10:14, 28), and lets Mark's own explanation carry the sense. The verb from the same root, koinoō, is "make unclean" in 7:15–23, as in Matthew 15:11–20.

p: Mark speaks to outsiders and paints with a broad brush. Not every Jew of the time kept this custom.
b: Mark writes for readers who are not Jews, probably in Rome, and he explains Jewish customs as a guide would (compare 14:12; 15:42). "All the Jews" is a broad statement. E. P. Sanders argued that washing hands before ordinary meals was a practice of the Pharisees and other very observant Jews, not yet a rule for all. Others think hand-washing was spreading widely, especially among Jews outside the land of Israel, who washed before prayer. Either way, Mark is not attacking Judaism here; he is explaining a custom so that his readers can follow the argument.

p: No one is sure what pygmē, "with a fist," means here. Some copyists changed it to "often."
b: Pygmē is the ordinary word for "fist," and it makes little sense with washing. Proposals: rubbing one fist in the palm of the other hand; pouring water over a cupped hand; washing "up to the wrist" (an old Greek explanation); or a handful of water, which matches the small measure the later Mishnah requires for rinsing hands (Mishnah Yadayim 1:1). Copyists were puzzled too: Codex Sinaiticus and Washington read pykna, "often" or "carefully," as the Latin Vulgate's crebro reflects, and a few witnesses leave the word out (as reported by Metzger). The Plain keeps the literal word, and the gloss gives the sense.

p: Mark uses baptizō, the word for baptism, for the dipping that kept things ritually pure.
b: The verb is baptizō, "dip, immerse," and the noun in the next sentence is baptismos. Jews of the time immersed in a ritual bath (Hebrew mikveh); many such stepped pools have been found in Judea and Galilee from the first century. A person back from the market, where he might have touched something impure, would immerse or wash before eating. Vessels were also immersed (Leviticus 11:32). Some early manuscripts read "sprinkle themselves" instead (see the variant). Mark's readers, who knew "baptism" as the Christian rite, would hear that the word had a Jewish life first (compare 1:4).

t: A Latin word in Mark's Greek
p: Xestēs is the Roman sextarius, a measure of about a pint. Mark uses several Latin words like it.
b: The Greek xestēs comes from the Latin sextarius, a jug holding about a pint. Mark has a number of such Latin loanwords: kentyriōn for centurion (15:39), kodrantēs for a small coin (12:42), praitōrion (15:16) and spekoulatōr for an executioner (6:27). Soldiers and traders spread these words across the eastern empire, so they do not prove a Roman origin. But they fit the early tradition, reported by Papias and later writers, that Mark wrote for Christians in Rome.

p: In Jewish speech, how you "walk" is how you live by God's law. The rabbis later called it halakhah.
b: The Pharisees literally ask why the disciples do not "walk according to" the tradition. The Hebrew Bible often speaks of walking in God's ways or laws (Exodus 16:4; Deuteronomy 8:6; Psalm 119:1). From the verb halakh, "walk," rabbis later named the practical rules of Jewish life halakhah, "the walking." So the question is not about manners but about the whole pattern of a faithful life. Paul uses the same picture for Christian living (Romans 6:4; Galatians 5:16).

p: A hypokritēs was a stage actor. Jesus calls the critics actors whose words and hearts do not match.
b: In Greek theater the hypokritēs was the actor, who spoke behind a mask. In the Greek Old Testament and in Jewish writings the word took on the sense of someone godless or false (Job 34:30; 36:13). Here it is Mark's only use of the noun, and Isaiah's words explain it at once: honor with the lips while the heart is far away. Jesus is not saying that all who keep the tradition are insincere; he is applying a prophet's charge to the people in front of him, as the prophets did to their own generation.

a: 'This people gives me honor with their lips
p: Jesus quotes Isaiah in the Greek version, which fits his point more sharply than the Hebrew does.
b: In the Hebrew of Isaiah 29:13, the prophet says the people's "fear of me / is a rule made by humans and learned by heart" (Isaiah 29:13). The Greek translation says that they worship God "in vain, teaching human commands and teachings," and Mark's quotation follows the Greek. The point is the same in both: worship turns hollow when human rules take the place of what God asked. Isaiah spoke to Jerusalem's leaders in the late 700s BC; Jesus applies his words to leaders of his own day, as Matthew 15:8–9 does in the same scene.

p: Mark has "Moses said"; Matthew has "God said." Both point to the Ten Words and to the law that protected them.
b: Jesus quotes the fifth of the Ten Words (Exodus 20:12; Deuteronomy 5:16) and Exodus 21:17. Mark's "Moses said" names the human lawgiver; Matthew 15:4 makes it "God said," stressing that this is God's own command set against human tradition. Mark makes the same point by calling it "God's command" (7:8–9) and "God's word" (7:13). The second quotation follows the Greek, "speaks evil of"; the Hebrew has "curses," which the site renders "Anyone who curses his father or his mother must be put to death" (Exodus 21:17). See the note at Matthew 15:4.

p: Mark keeps the Hebrew-Aramaic word and translates it. Saying "Korban" over something put it off limits.
b: Qorban is the Hebrew word for an offering brought near to God (Leviticus 1:2). By Jesus' time, saying "Korban!" over property was a vow formula: it made the thing like a Temple gift, forbidden to the person named, even if it never reached the altar. An ossuary lid found at Jebel Hallet et-Turi near Jerusalem bears the word qrbn, apparently to keep people from using what was inside, as Joseph Fitzmyer showed. A son could use such a vow against his parents. The Mishnah later allows a vow like this to be undone when it harms one's father and mother (Mishnah Nedarim 9:1), so Jesus' side of the argument is the one later Jewish law took.

p: Jesus attacks a tradition that cancels a command of God. Readers differ on how far his criticism reaches.
b: The "tradition of the elders" became what later rabbis called the Oral Torah, collected in the Mishnah about AD 200 (Mishnah Avot 1:1). Some readers take Jesus to reject the oral tradition as such. Most scholars, Jewish and Christian, think he rejects particular rulings that let human rules override God's written word, as here, much as the Sadducees rejected the Pharisees' traditions for their own reasons. Christians later used this passage in their own arguments over Scripture and church tradition; the card at Matthew 15 sets out how the churches answer.

p: The KJV's "all the people" follows the Byzantine text, which reads panta, "all," for palin, "again."
b: The two Greek words look alike (palin, panta), and a copyist could easily read one for the other. NA28, the SBLGNT, the Tyndale House GNT and Westcott-Hort print "again," a word Mark often uses to link scenes (7:31; 8:1; 8:13). A small difference of the same kind explains the KJV's "straightway" at 7:35: the Byzantine text has "immediately," which NA28 and the SBLGNT do not print. Neither changes the sense.

a: Nothing that enters a person from outside has the power to make him unclean.
p: Jesus' riddle about what defiles has been read as ending the purity laws, as ranking them, or as a point about hands.
b: Ending purity laws: most Christian readers, following Mark's own comment in 7:19, take the saying to set aside the laws of clean and unclean food. Ranking, not ending: Geza Vermes and James Dunn read it as a Hebrew way of saying "not so much this as that": moral impurity matters far more than ritual impurity, as the prophets taught (Hosea 6:6). About hands and food: Yair Furstenberg argues that the Pharisees held a newer view, that impurity from unwashed hands passes into the food and so into the body. Jesus defends the older biblical view that impurity comes from outside sources and does not enter through eating. On this reading he is defending the Torah against an innovation.

p: In Mark a parable can be a single riddling saying. Jesus explains it in private, as in chapter 4.
b: Parabolē renders the Hebrew mashal, which covers proverbs, riddles and short sayings as well as stories. Jesus has just spoken a riddle (7:15). As with the parables by the lake (4:10–20, 33–34), the explanation comes indoors, to the disciples alone. Mark's pattern of public riddle and private teaching invites his own readers inside the house too.

p: Most read this as Mark's own comment that Jesus' words ended the food laws. Some read it differently.
b: Mark's comment: most scholars (Marcus, Collins, France) take the phrase as Mark's aside to his Gentile readers: Jesus' teaching means that no food is unclean for believers, as Peter learned in his vision (Acts 10:15) and Paul taught (Romans 14:14, 20). A statement about digestion: Daniel Boyarin argues that the participle goes with the latrine: the body's own process purges all food, so food cannot defile; Jesus, a Torah-keeping Jew, is arguing against a Pharisaic purity rule, not against kosher law. About purity of food, not kinds of food: David Rudolph argues the comment concerns food made impure by unwashed hands, not pork or shellfish. Matthew leaves the comment out (Matthew 15:17). See the variant, and the food-laws card at Matthew 15.

t: A list of vices from the heart
p: Mark lists twelve wrongs, six plural acts and six singular attitudes. Matthew trims it and orders it like the commandments.
b: Lists of vices were common in Greek moral writing and in Jewish texts such as the Community Rule from Qumran (1QS 4:9–11) and Wisdom of Solomon 14:25–26 (a book in Catholic and Orthodox Bibles), and Paul uses them (Romans 1:29–31; Galatians 5:19–21). Mark's has twelve items: first six plural deeds (sexual immorality, thefts, murders, adulteries, acts of greed, wicked acts), then six singular dispositions (deceit, indecency, envy, slander, arrogance, senselessness). Matthew 15:19 keeps six, in the order of the commandments (murder, adultery, theft, false witness), with sexual immorality and slanders. The point is the heart, the center of thought and will in biblical speech (Jeremiah 17:9; Genesis 6:5).

t: An evil eye: envy and stinginess
p: Not a curse or magic here. In Jewish idiom an evil eye is grudging envy, the opposite of a generous eye.
b: In the Hebrew Bible a person with "an evil eye" is stingy and resentful (Deuteronomy 15:9; Proverbs 23:6; Proverbs 28:22), while "a good eye" is generous (Proverbs 22:9). Jesus uses the idiom again in Matthew 20:15, where the landowner asks, in effect, "Are you envious because I am generous?" Belief in the evil eye as a harmful glance was also widespread in the ancient world, but the list here is about attitudes, and envy is the sense.

a: He went into a house and wanted no one to find out he was there
p: Tyre was a rich Gentile port. Jesus goes there to be hidden, and is found by a Gentile mother.
b: Tyre, on the coast of today's Lebanon, was an old Phoenician city, rich from trade and from the purple-dye industry. Its farmland was small, and it bought grain from Galilee (compare Acts 12:20). Gerd Theissen suggests that the story's talk of "the children's bread" would sting in that setting: Galilean villagers often felt that rich Gentile cities took their food. Jesus' wish to stay hidden fits Mark's pattern of secrecy (1:44; 5:43; 7:36), and Mark notes that it fails, as it usually does.

p: "Greek" marks her culture and religion; "Syrophoenician" her people. Matthew calls her a Canaanite.
b: "Greek" (Hellēnis) here means a Gentile who spoke Greek and lived by Greek ways, perhaps a woman of some standing. "Syrophoenician" distinguished Phoenicians of the Roman province of Syria from the "Libyphoenicians" of North Africa around Carthage, a Roman way of speaking that may again reflect Mark's Roman setting. Matthew 15:22 uses the old biblical name "Canaanite." In both Gospels the point is the same: she is as far outside Israel as a neighbor can be.

a: Allow the children to eat their fill first.
p: Only Mark has "first." It leaves room for the Gentiles after Israel, as Paul's "to the Jew first" does.
b: The "children" are Israel, God's children (Exodus 4:22; Deuteronomy 14:1); the "bread" is what Jesus brings, healing and the kingdom, just after he has fed five thousand in Galilee (6:30–44). Mark alone includes "first": the order is Israel, then the nations, as Paul puts it, "first for the Jew and for the Greek as well" (Romans 1:16). The woman accepts the order and asks only for what falls from the table now. Matthew drops "first" but adds "I have not been sent to anyone but the sheep of the house of Israel that are lost" (Matthew 15:24).

p: Jesus' words sound harsh to modern ears, and readers have long argued over them. See also Matthew 15:26.
b: Kynaria is a diminutive, which many read as "house dogs" rather than street scavengers; whether the diminutive still softened the word in everyday Greek is debated. Even so, "dogs" could be an insult for Gentiles (compare Philippians 3:2, where Paul turns it around). Readings: a test that draws out her faith (Chrysostom); a proverb about order at a family table, not contempt ("first" in this verse); Jesus changed by her answer, a reading developed by Sharon Ringe and many other modern and feminist interpreters; a lesson about the disciples, as in Matthew. Whatever the intent, Mark presents a Gentile mother who answers Jesus wisely and wins her request.

t: The only one who calls Jesus "Lord"
p: In Mark no one else addresses Jesus as "Lord." On her lips it may be a polite "sir," but Mark's readers heard more.
b: Kyrie was a polite address, "sir," as well as a title for God and, among Christians, for Jesus. In Mark the disciples call Jesus "Teacher" or "Rabbi"; this Gentile woman is the only person in the Gospel who speaks to him as Kyrie. She also takes his own image and turns it into her plea. Mark's Gentile readers, who confessed "Jesus is Lord" (1 Corinthians 12:3), would hear their own confession in her mouth.

p: Mark praises the woman's word; Matthew her great faith. Both say her answer is what moved Jesus.
b: Mark has Jesus say, literally, "Because of this word, go." Matthew 15:28 makes it "your faith is great." Mark's form puts the stress on her reply itself: she argued with Jesus and won. She is one of several people in Mark who come from outside and understand more than the insiders (5:18–20; 12:34; 15:39). In the next chapter the disciples, who have eaten their fill twice, still do not understand about the bread (8:14–21). The healing happens at a distance, as with the centurion's servant in Matthew 8:13.

a: to the Sea of Galilee, in the middle of the Decapolis territory
p: Going from Tyre by way of Sidon to the lake is a long loop north and then southeast. Readers explain it differently.
b: Sidon lies about 20 miles north of Tyre, and the Sea of Galilee lies to the southeast, so the route described is a wide circuit. Some critics conclude that Mark, or his source, did not know Galilean geography well. Others (Gundry, France) take it as a real, long journey through Gentile lands, perhaps months of travel, which Mark summarizes. A literary reading sees a deliberate tour of Gentile territory: Tyre, Sidon and the Ten Cities, where the healed man of 5:20 had already spread the news. Copyists smoothed the route (see the variant).

a: a deaf man who struggled to speak
p: Mogilalos appears nowhere else in the Bible except the Greek of Isaiah 35:6. Mark is pointing at Isaiah's promise.
b: The word mogilalos, "speaking with difficulty," is found in the Greek Bible only here and in Isaiah 35:6. Isaiah pictured God coming to save his people: "Then blind people's eyes will open, / and deaf people's ears will be unplugged" (Isaiah 35:5), and the tongue that could not speak would sing. The crowd's cry in 7:37 picks up the same promise, and Mark tells the healing of a blind man soon after (8:22–26). Jesus' answer to John in Matthew 11:5 uses the same chapter of Isaiah.

p: Saliva was a known healing remedy in the ancient world. Jesus uses touch and spit, as a healer might, and then a word.
b: Ancient writers mention saliva as a cure. Tacitus reports that the emperor Vespasian, at Alexandria, was asked to heal a blind man by spreading his spittle on his eyes (Histories 4.81), and Pliny the Elder lists uses of saliva in medicine. Jesus' actions here and in 8:23 are physical and private, almost like sign language for a man who cannot hear: fingers to the ears, a touch on the tongue, a look to heaven. Matthew and Luke leave out both of Mark's spittle healings, perhaps because the methods looked too much like a wonder-worker's.

p: Mark keeps Jesus' own Aramaic word and translates it. The early church used it in baptism.
b: Ephphatha represents the Aramaic ethpattach (or a Hebrew form), "be opened." Mark keeps several of Jesus' Aramaic words and translates them for his Greek-speaking readers: talitha koum (5:41), Korban (7:11), Abba (14:36), Eloi (15:34). Ambrose of Milan describes a rite in which the bishop touched the ears and nose of those about to be baptized, saying "Ephphatha" (On the Mysteries 1.3), and a form of this "Ephphatha" prayer remains an optional part of the Catholic rite of baptism. The healing became a picture of a person opened to hear God's word.

p: Stenazō is a deep sigh or groan. It may be prayer, compassion, or the strain of the struggle with illness.
b: The verb means to sigh or groan deeply. It may express prayer (Romans 8:23, 26 use the same word group for creation's and the Spirit's groaning), sorrow over the man's suffering, or the effort of a healer facing a hostile power. Mark uses a stronger form of it in 8:12, where Jesus groans at the Pharisees' demand for a sign. Mark often shows Jesus' emotions, which Matthew and Luke tend to leave out (compare 1:41; 3:5; 10:14).

a: the more widely they proclaimed it
t: A secret that will not stay kept
p: Jesus orders silence; the people "proclaim" all the more, using Mark's word for preaching.
b: This is part of what William Wrede (1901) called Mark's "messianic secret": Jesus forbids people to spread news of his deeds or his identity (1:34, 44; 3:12; 5:43; 8:30; 9:9). Wrede thought Mark built the theme to explain why Jesus was not recognized as Messiah in his lifetime. Many scholars today see real caution by Jesus behind it, sharpened by Mark's storytelling: Jesus can be understood only in light of the cross. Here the secret breaks, and the verb is kēryssō, "proclaim," Mark's word for preaching the good news (1:14; 13:10).

a: All that he has done, he has done well
p: The crowd's words echo creation, when God saw that everything he had made was very good.
b: Many interpreters hear Genesis 1:31 here, where God looked at all he had made and it was very good; the Greek of Genesis uses the same word, kalos. Healing a deaf and speechless man is a small act of new creation. The second half of the cry repeats Isaiah 35:5–6: the deaf hear and the speechless speak, signs that God has come to save (see the note at 7:32). People who are probably Gentiles, in the Ten Cities, are the ones who say it.

a: In those days a big crowd was with him again
p: Mark tells two feedings, as Matthew does. Some see one event told twice; some see a meal for Gentiles.
b: Readers have long asked why the disciples, who saw five thousand fed (6:30–44), ask "Where could anyone get bread?" (8:4). Many critical scholars think one event came down in two versions. Traditional readers, from Augustine on, take them as two events, as Jesus' own words in 8:19–20 assume. Many readers notice the setting: after Tyre, Sidon and the Ten Cities (7:24–31), this crowd was probably largely Gentile. On the numbers of baskets, see 8:19; on the disciples' slowness, 8:17–21.

a: Some of them have traveled from far off.
p: Only Mark has this line. "Those far off" was a biblical way of speaking of the nations.
b: In the Greek Old Testament, people who come "from far off" are often foreigners (Joshua 9:6; Isaiah 60:4). Christian writers picked up the phrase for Gentile believers, who were once "far off" (Acts 2:39; Ephesians 2:13). Some scholars think Mark's phrase hints that the crowd includes Gentiles. Others read it simply as a practical concern: people who walked a long way would faint on the road home.

t: The words of the Lord's Supper
p: Took, gave thanks, broke, gave: Mark uses the same actions as at the Last Supper.
b: Here Jesus "gave thanks" (eucharisteō, the source of the word Eucharist), where in the first feeding he "said the blessing" (6:41). Both are Jewish table blessings: Jews thanked God over bread before a meal. At the Last Supper Mark uses both verbs (14:22–23). Christians reading Mark in their own gatherings would hear in this desert meal a picture of the bread they broke together. The meal also recalls God feeding Israel with manna in the wilderness (Exodus 16).

p: The Pharisees want a sign that would prove Jesus came from God. Other would-be leaders of the time promised such signs.
b: A "sign from heaven" means proof from God, perhaps a wonder in the sky. Josephus tells of men in the following decades who promised signs: Theudas said he would part the Jordan (Antiquities 20.97–98), and a prophet from Egypt said Jerusalem's walls would fall at his command (Antiquities 20.169–172); the Romans killed their followers. Jesus has done many acts of power, but he refuses to give a sign on demand. "Putting him to the test" is the verb used of Satan's testing in the wilderness (1:13).

a: this generation will get no sign at all
p: Jesus speaks in the form of a Hebrew oath. Mark has no "sign of Jonah," as Matthew and Luke do.
b: Literally Jesus says, "if a sign shall be given to this generation!" This copies a Hebrew oath, im, "if," with the curse left unsaid: "May I be cursed if..." It is the strongest possible no (compare Psalm 95:11, quoted in Hebrews 3:11). Matthew 12:39 and 16:4 and Luke 11:29 add "except the sign of Jonah"; Mark gives a flat refusal. "This generation" echoes the faithless wilderness generation (Deuteronomy 32:5; Psalm 95:10).
r: Psalm 95:10–11; Hebrews 3:11; Deuteronomy 32:5; Matthew 12:39; Matthew 16:4; Luke 11:29

p: Only Mark mentions the single loaf. Some readers think it points to Jesus himself.
b: Mark alone says the disciples had "one loaf" in the boat. Read plainly, it explains their worry: one loaf for thirteen men. Some interpreters see more: the disciples fret about bread while the one who fed thousands sits with them, the "one loaf" they overlook (compare 1 Corinthians 10:17, "we, though many, are one body, for we all share the one loaf"). That is a reading, not something the text states; Mark leaves the riddle open, as Jesus does in 8:21.

t: Yeast: a small thing that spreads
p: Yeast works unseen through a whole batch of dough. Jesus warns of an influence spreading among his own followers.
b: Yeast (leaven) was a lump of old fermented dough. At Passover, Israel removed it from every home (Exodus 12:15–20), and Paul uses it as a picture of corruption that spreads (1 Corinthians 5:6–8; Galatians 5:9). Jesus' warning pairs the Pharisees with Herod Antipas, who had John the Baptist killed (6:14–29); Pharisees and Herod's supporters already plotted together (3:6) and will test Jesus again (12:13). What is the yeast? Mark does not say. Readers suggest unbelief that demands signs (8:11), or hardness of heart (3:5–6; 8:17). Matthew 16:12 explains it as teaching.

p: Mark uses the same word for the disciples that he used for Jesus' opponents in 3:5.
b: The verb pōroō means to harden, to grow a callus. Mark used the related noun for the Pharisees' hardness in 3:5 and said of the disciples after the walking on water, "their hearts had turned hard" (6:52). Now Jesus asks it of them directly, and in 8:18 he applies to them the prophets' words about people with eyes and ears who do not see or hear, words Mark earlier used of "those outside" (4:11–12). Mark does not flatter the Twelve; his readers, facing their own failures, could see that Jesus kept teaching them.

a: With eyes, you don't see? With ears, you don't hear?
p: Jesus uses the words of Jeremiah and Ezekiel, spoken about a stubborn Israel, of his own disciples.
b: Jeremiah 5:21 speaks to a foolish people who have eyes but do not see and ears but do not hear, and Ezekiel 12:2 calls Israel "a rebellious house" with the same blindness and deafness. Isaiah 6:9–10, which Jesus quoted about outsiders in 4:12, belongs to the same family of sayings. Mark sets this question just before Jesus heals a blind man in two stages (8:22–26) and right after he opened a deaf man's ears (7:31–37). The healings show what Jesus must still do for the disciples.

a: How many baskets full of pieces did you pick up?
p: Jesus quizzes the disciples on the numbers. Mark never gives the answer to his riddle.
b: Mark keeps two different words: kophinos, a small basket, for the twelve (6:43), and spyris, a large hamper, for the seven (8:8). Jesus asks the numbers as though they were the key. A common reading, from early church writers to modern scholars, takes twelve for Israel's tribes and seven for the nations (the seven nations of Canaan, Deuteronomy 7:1 and Acts 13:19; the seven Greek-speaking helpers of Acts 6:3; or the number of completeness), so that Jesus' bread is for both. Others think the point is simpler: the leftovers prove there is more than enough, so worrying over one loaf is foolish. The question "Don't you understand yet?" (8:21) is left hanging for the reader.

p: A fishing town at the north end of the lake, in Philip's territory. Two sites compete to be it.
b: Bethsaida ("house of fishing") lay near where the Jordan enters the Sea of Galilee, in the territory of Herod Philip, who rebuilt it and renamed it Julias (Josephus, Antiquities 18.28). John 1:44 makes it the home of Philip, Andrew and Peter. Its site is debated: excavations at et-Tell, a mound about 1.5 miles from the shore, and since 2016 at el-Araj, nearer the lake, where a Roman-period settlement and a Byzantine church have been found. Mark calls it a "village" (8:23, 26), though Josephus says Philip made it a city.

a: He spat into the man's eyes
t: Two healings Matthew and Luke leave out
p: Mark's healings of the deaf man and the blind man are missing from Matthew and Luke. Scholars ask why.
b: Matthew and Luke follow most of Mark, but neither tells the healing of the deaf man (7:31–37) or this one. Both involve spit, private actions and, here, a healing that takes two tries. Many scholars think the later Gospels found these details awkward: they could make Jesus look like a magician or seem to struggle. Others note that Matthew summarizes healings of the deaf and blind instead (Matthew 15:30–31). For Mark the details carry meaning (see 8:24). This is one of the standard pieces of evidence in the debate over which Gospel came first; see the topic page on the Synoptic problem.

a: I can see them as trees, walking around
p: The only healing in the Gospels that happens in stages. Mark sets it just before Peter half-sees who Jesus is.
b: Read as history, the man first sees blurred shapes, which suggests he once had sight and has to learn again what he sees. Read as Mark's story, the timing matters: this healing comes right after Jesus asks "Don't you understand yet?" (8:21) and right before Peter rightly calls Jesus the Messiah but cannot accept that he must suffer (8:29–33). The disciples see, but only partly, like men seeing people as trees. On how this healing opens the road section (8:22–10:52), see the chapter page.

p: The verb apokathistēmi, "restore," returns in 9:12, where Elijah "sets everything right again."
b: Apekatestē, "he was restored," is the verb used of a withered hand restored (3:5) and of Elijah who "sets everything right again" (9:12; Malachi 4:6 in the Greek). The man "looked intently" and then saw "everything plainly, even at a distance" (tēlaugōs, "far-shining"). Across 8:24–25 Mark uses three verbs of seeing: the man "looked up" (anablepsas), "looked intently" (dieblepsen) and "could make out" (eneblepen), a picture of full sight after the half-sight of 8:24.

p: A Gentile city at the source of the Jordan, with a cave shrine to the god Pan and a temple to Augustus.
b: Herod Philip rebuilt the town of Paneas, at the foot of Mount Hermon, and renamed it Caesarea in honor of the emperor (Josephus, Antiquities 18.28). It had a cave shrine of Pan and a white marble temple Herod the Great built for Augustus (Antiquities 15.363–364). Jesus asks who he is in the countryside of a city named for Caesar. See the note at Matthew 16:13.

p: Hodos means both "road" and "way." From here to 10:52 Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem.
b: Hodos is the ordinary word for a road, and also for a way of life. Mark opens with Isaiah's call to get the Lord's road ready (1:2–3). Now the word keeps returning: the disciples argue on the road (9:33–34); a rich man runs up as Jesus sets out on the road (10:17); Jesus walks ahead of them on the road up to Jerusalem (10:32); Bartimaeus follows him on the road (10:52). English Bibles that switch between "road," "way" and "journey" hide the thread; the Plain keeps "road." On how the whole section is built, see the chapter page.

p: The same three answers Herod's court gave in 6:14–15: John raised, Elijah, a prophet.
b: Mark has already listed these opinions when Herod heard of Jesus (6:14–16): some said John the Baptist had been raised, some said Elijah, some a prophet like the old prophets. Elijah was expected to return before the day of the LORD (Malachi 4:5); see 9:11–13. All three answers place Jesus among God's messengers. Peter's answer goes beyond them.

t: Peter's confession, in its shortest form
p: Mark has no "Son of the living God" and no "on this rock." Readers explain the difference in several ways.
b: Christos is Greek for the Hebrew mashiach, "anointed one," the king God would send (Psalm 2:2). In Mark, Peter says only this; Matthew 16:16–19 adds "the Son of the living God" and Jesus' blessing, new name and keys for Peter; Luke 9:20 has "God's Messiah." Most scholars think Mark is the earlier form and Matthew expanded it. An old tradition, found in Eusebius (Proof of the Gospel 3.5), explains Mark's silence by Peter's modesty, since Mark wrote down Peter's preaching. Mark's own point follows at once: Peter has the right title but the wrong idea of it (8:31–33). On Peter and the papacy, see the card at Matthew 16:18.

p: The same verb, epitimaō, three times: Jesus rebukes the disciples, Peter rebukes Jesus, Jesus rebukes Peter.
b: Epitimaō is a strong word. Jesus "rebukes" demons (1:25; 3:12; 9:25) and the wind (4:39) with it. In 8:30–33 it falls three times: Jesus rebukes the disciples to keep silent, Peter rebukes Jesus for speaking of suffering, and Jesus rebukes Peter as "Satan." The chain shows the clash of two ideas of Messiah, a contest Mark presents almost as a struggle with an evil power. Many English Bibles soften the first one to "warned"; in 8:30–33 the Plain keeps "rebuke" all three times. Mark uses the verb again in 10:13 and 10:48, where the Plain fits the English to the scene.

a: the Son of Man had to suffer much
p: Jesus now says plainly that the Son of Man must suffer, die and rise. He will say it twice more.
b: "Had to" is dei, "it is necessary," the language of God's plan (compare 9:11; 13:10; 14:31). This is the first of three predictions (8:31; 9:31; 10:33–34); on the pattern they share, see the chapter page. Many critical scholars think the detailed wording was shaped after Easter; others hold that Jesus, who saw what happened to John (6:17–29) and to prophets before him, foresaw his death and spoke of it. "The Son of Man" is Jesus' usual way of speaking of himself; see the topic page and Daniel 7:13–14.

a: thrown out by the elders, the chief priests and the scribes
t: The stone the builders threw out
p: "Thrown out" is the verb of Psalm 118:22, which Jesus quotes in 12:10. The three groups made up the council.
b: Apodokimazō means to reject after testing, as a builder rejects a stone. The Greek of Psalm 118:22 uses it: "A stone that the builders threw out / has become the head of the corner" (Psalm 118:22). Jesus will quote that psalm after the parable of the tenants (12:10), and the early church used it often (Acts 4:11; 1 Peter 2:7). The elders, chief priests and scribes together formed the council that tries Jesus (14:53; 15:1).

p: Mark says "after three days"; Matthew and Luke say "on the third day." In Jewish counting these meant the same.
b: Mark's three predictions say "after three days" (8:31; 9:31; 10:34) in the oldest manuscripts; the KJV's "the third day" at 9:31 and 10:34 comes from later copies (see the variants). Matthew 16:21 and Luke 9:22 change it to "on the third day," the form of the early creed (1 Corinthians 15:4). In Jewish reckoning part of a day counted as a day, so the phrases overlap: Esther fasts "three days" and goes to the king "on the third day" (Esther 4:16; Esther 5:1). Hosea 6:2 joins both: "after two days ... on the third day." Mark also has Jesus "rise" (active), where Matthew and Luke have "be raised."
orig: μετὰ τρεῖς ἡμέρας ἀναστῆναι (meta treis hēmeras anastēnai)
r: Matthew 16:21; Luke 9:22; 1 Corinthians 15:4; Hosea 6:2; Esther 4:16; Esther 5:1; 14:58; 15:29

a: He was speaking the message openly
p: Parrēsia, "openly, boldly." Up to now Jesus spoke in parables; about his death he speaks plainly.
b: Parrēsia means frankness, saying everything. Jesus has taught the crowds "in parables" (4:33–34) and ordered silence about his deeds and identity. About his suffering he holds nothing back. "The message" (ho logos, literally "the word") is Mark's term for what Jesus preached (2:2; 4:33), so his coming death is now part of the message itself. Acts uses the same word for the apostles' bold preaching (Acts 4:29–31).

a: looked at his disciples and rebuked Peter
p: Jesus looks at all the disciples and rebukes Peter. Peter is speaking for them, and in Satan's role.
b: Only Mark says Jesus "looked at his disciples" before rebuking Peter: the rebuke is meant for the whole group. "Satan" was the one who tested Jesus in the wilderness (1:12–13), offering, in Matthew and Luke, glory without the cross; Peter now tempts him the same way. "Get behind me" (opisō mou) uses the words of the call, "Come behind me" (1:17), and of 8:34: Peter is sent back to a follower's place. Mark's frank picture of Peter fits the early tradition that Peter's own preaching lay behind this Gospel.

a: He called the crowd over, along with his disciples
p: The call to carry the cross goes to the crowd, not only to the Twelve. A cross meant a Roman execution.
b: Jesus addresses this saying to the crowd as well as the disciples: the way is open to anyone. A condemned man carried the crossbeam of his own cross to the place of execution (15:21; John 19:17), so "pick up his cross" pictures a man walking to his death. Galileans had seen it: Roman forces crucified rebels in Galilee and Judea. Mark's first readers, if they lived in Rome, had seen it too: Tacitus says that after the fire of AD 64 Nero had Christians crucified or set alight (Annals 15.44).
r: 15:21; Matthew 10:38; Matthew 16:24; Luke 9:23; Luke 14:27; John 19:17; Galatians 2:20

a: because of me and the good news
p: Only Mark adds "and the good news" here and in 10:29. For his readers, dying for Jesus meant dying for the gospel.
b: Euangelion, "good news," is Mark's word: his book begins "The beginning of the good news" (1:1), and Jesus announces the good news of God (1:14–15). Matthew 16:25 and Luke 9:24 say only "because of me." Mark's fuller form speaks to readers who might lose their lives for proclaiming the message (13:9–10). "Life" here is psychē, which means both life and soul; see the note at Matthew 16:25.
orig: ἕνεκεν ἐμοῦ καὶ τοῦ εὐαγγελίου (heneken emou kai tou euangeliou)

a: ashamed of me and my words
p: A warning for disciples under pressure. Matthew and Luke have a form of it with "deny" instead.
b: Mark's readers lived in a world where a crucified Messiah was a shameful thing to confess (1 Corinthians 1:23; Romans 1:16, "I am not ashamed of the good news"). Jesus warns that those ashamed of him before people will find the Son of Man ashamed of them. Luke 9:26 keeps the same form; Matthew 10:32–33 and Luke 12:8–9 have a parallel saying about acknowledging and denying. "Adulterous" is the prophets' word for a people unfaithful to God, as a wife to her husband (Hosea 2:2–5; Matthew 12:39).
r: Romans 1:16; 2 Timothy 1:8; 2 Timothy 2:12; Luke 9:26; Matthew 10:32–33; Luke 12:8–9; Hosea 2:2–5; Matthew 12:39

a: when he comes in the glory of his Father, along with the holy angels
t: The Son of Man in glory
p: The first time Mark speaks of the Son of Man coming in glory. The picture comes from Daniel 7.
b: In Daniel's vision "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds of heaven and receives everlasting rule (Daniel 7:13–14), and myriads of angels stand before God (Daniel 7:10). Mark returns to this picture in 13:26 and in Jesus' answer to the high priest (14:62). The same Son of Man who must be "thrown out" (8:31) will come as judge. "His Father" quietly identifies the Son of Man as God's Son, as the voice will do in 9:7.

a: some who will never taste death before they see the kingdom of God arrived in power
p: What did some of those listening see before they died? Five main answers have been given.
b: The transfiguration, which Mark tells next, "six days later" (9:2): the common view of the church fathers, supported by 2 Peter 1:16–18. The resurrection and Pentecost, when the kingdom came in power (Romans 1:4; Acts 1:8). The fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, as God's judgment and Jesus' vindication (compare 13:30). The spread of the church. The final coming, expected soon, which Albert Schweitzer and others conclude did not come as Jesus expected. Mark's perfect participle, "having come," stresses a kingdom that will be seen as already arrived. On Matthew's form, see the note at Matthew 16:28.

t: Six days, a high mountain, three friends
p: The details recall Moses on Sinai. Peter, James and John are the three who see the most and the worst.
b: On Sinai the cloud covered the mountain "six days," and on the seventh God called to Moses out of the cloud (Exodus 24:15–16); Moses went up with chosen companions (Exodus 24:1, 9). Here a cloud and a voice follow too (9:7). Peter, James and John are with Jesus at the raising of Jairus' daughter (5:37) and will be nearest him in Gethsemane (14:33): they see his glory and his anguish. See the note at Matthew 17:1.

p: Metamorphoō: changed in form. Paul uses the same verb for believers being changed into Christ's image.
b: The verb gives English "metamorphosis"; Latin Bibles render it transfiguratus, hence "transfiguration." Mark describes only the clothes (9:3); Matthew 17:2 and Luke 9:29 add that his face shone, like Moses' face after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29–35). Paul uses the same verb for believers "being transformed into the same image" (2 Corinthians 3:18) and "be transformed instead, by the renewing of your mind" (Romans 12:2). On how the churches understand the light, see the card on the chapter page.

a: whiter than any cloth-bleacher on earth could make them
p: A fuller cleaned and whitened new wool cloth. Mark's homely comparison makes the glory something no human work could make.
b: A fuller (gnapheus) washed, beat and bleached wool, often with lye or chalk, to make it white; Jerusalem had a "Fuller's Field" (Isaiah 7:3). Mark says no fuller on earth could get cloth this white: the brightness comes from heaven. White clothing marks heavenly beings: the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9, the young man at the tomb (16:5), the angels and the redeemed in Revelation (Revelation 3:4–5; Revelation 7:9). The Byzantine text adds "as snow" (see the variant).

p: Mark names Elijah first. Both met God on a mountain, and both had mysterious ends.
b: Matthew and Luke write "Moses and Elijah"; Mark puts Elijah first, perhaps because the conversation that follows is about Elijah (9:11–13). Many readers see the Law and the Prophets standing with Jesus. Both men met God on Sinai, also called Horeb (Exodus 24; Exodus 33:18–23; 1 Kings 19:8–13), both suffered for God's word, and both had unusual ends: no one knew Moses' grave (Deuteronomy 34:6), and Elijah was taken up in a whirlwind (2 Kings 2:11). Jewish tradition expected Elijah, and some texts a prophet like Moses, before the end (Malachi 4:4–6; Deuteronomy 18:15).
r: Exodus 33:18–23; 1 Kings 19:8–13; Deuteronomy 34:6; 2 Kings 2:11; Malachi 4:4–6; Deuteronomy 18:15; Matthew 17:3

p: In Mark, Peter says "Rabbi." Matthew has "Lord" and Luke "Master," a pattern scholars use to compare the Gospels.
b: Rabbi, "my great one," was a respectful address for a teacher; later it became a title for ordained Jewish teachers. In Mark, Peter calls Jesus Rabbi here and in 11:21, and Judas uses it at the arrest (14:45). At this point Matthew 17:4 has "Lord" and Luke 9:33 "Master." Many scholars see a pattern: the later Gospels raise the title Mark's characters use. Mark's disciples speak as followers of a Jewish teacher.

a: He did not know what answer to give
p: Only Mark explains Peter's offer by his terror. Mark's portrait of Peter is frank throughout.
b: Peter's offer to build booths, shelters like those of the Feast of Booths (Leviticus 23:42–43), may mean he wants to keep the moment, or to honor three equals. Mark adds that he spoke out of fear and did not know what to say, as the disciples later "did not know what to answer" in Gethsemane (14:40). Matthew omits the explanation; Luke 9:33 says "He had no idea what he was saying." The tradition that Mark wrote down Peter's own preaching would make this a story Peter told against himself. See the note at Matthew 17:4 on the booths.

a: This is my dearly loved Son. Listen to him!
t: The voice, for the second time
p: At the baptism the voice spoke to Jesus; now it speaks to the disciples. It adds Moses' words, "Listen to him."
b: At the baptism the voice said "You are my dearly loved Son" to Jesus alone (1:11). Here it speaks about him to the three. The words draw on Psalm 2:7, the king as God's son; on Genesis 22:2, Abraham's "only one, whom you love"; and on Deuteronomy 18:15, where Moses says of the prophet God will raise up: "You must listen to him" (Deuteronomy 18:15). Coming just after Peter rejected Jesus' talk of suffering, "Listen to him" means listen to that too. Demons have already called him God's Son (3:11; 5:7), and the high priest will ask it (14:61), but after the baptism and the mountain the next voice to say it outright is a human one: the centurion's at the cross (15:39).
r: 1:11; 3:11; 5:7; 14:61; 15:39; Psalm 2:7; Genesis 22:2; Deuteronomy 18:15; Isaiah 42:1; 2 Peter 1:17–18; Matthew 17:5

a: not until the Son of Man had risen from among the dead
t: A secret with a time limit
p: The silence Jesus orders ends at the resurrection. William Wrede built his theory of the messianic secret on this verse.
b: This is the only command to silence in Mark that comes with an end date. Wrede took it as the key to the "messianic secret": in his view, Mark's church knew Jesus as Messiah only after Easter, and Mark explained the gap by having Jesus keep it secret until then. Many scholars accept that Mark shapes the theme but think it reflects real history too: who Jesus was could not be understood apart from the cross and resurrection. Either way, readers learn why Jesus' glory had to stay hidden: it would be misread until he had suffered.

a: to rise from among the dead
p: Many Jews expected the dead to rise at the end of the age. One man rising before the end was a new idea.
b: Daniel 12:2 speaks of many who sleep in the dust awaking, some to everlasting life, and the Pharisees taught a resurrection at the end of the age (12:18–27; Acts 23:8). What puzzled the disciples was resurrection "from among the dead": one man raised while the rest stay in their graves, before the end has come. Paul later explains it as "the first fruits" of the harvest (1 Corinthians 15:20–23).

a: Why do the scribes say Elijah has to come first?
p: Malachi promised that God would send Elijah before the great day of the LORD. Jewish teachers expected him.
b: The last words of the prophets in the Christian order of the Old Testament promise that God will send Elijah before the day of the LORD, to turn the hearts of parents and children to each other (Malachi 4:5–6, Malachi 3:23–24 in Hebrew Bibles). Sirach 48:10 says Elijah will "restore the tribes of Jacob." The Mishnah records later debate over what Elijah will do when he comes, ending with the view that he will come to make peace in the world (Mishnah Eduyot 8:7). At the Passover meal Jews still set a cup and open the door for Elijah. The disciples ask: if Elijah has not come, how can the end be here?
r: Malachi 4:5–6; Sirach 48:10; Luke 1:17; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:10; John 1:21

p: No single verse says the Son of Man will suffer. Jesus draws on Isaiah 53 and the Psalms of the righteous sufferer.
b: Exoudeneō means to treat as nothing, to despise. Isaiah's servant was one "we counted ... as nothing" (Isaiah 53:3), and the Greek of Psalm 118:22, quoted with this verb in Acts 4:11, speaks of the stone the builders threw out. In Psalm 22:6 the sufferer is "a thing for people to insult." Daniel's "one like a son of man" stands for God's holy people, who suffer before they receive the kingdom (Daniel 7:21–27). Jesus joins these threads: before the glory, the Son of Man must suffer.

p: Mark does not name him, but the Elijah who came and suffered is John the Baptist.
b: Matthew 17:13 spells it out: the disciples understood he meant John the Baptist. Mark leaves it to the reader, who remembers John dressed like Elijah (1:6; 2 Kings 1:8) and killed at the wish of Herodias (6:17–29), much as Jezebel sought Elijah's life (1 Kings 19:2, 10). "As the Scriptures say of him" is a puzzle, since no verse says Elijah will suffer; most think Jesus means the Elijah story itself, read as a pattern. Luke 1:17 says John would walk ahead of the Lord "with Elijah's spirit and power"; in John 1:21, John denies being Elijah, perhaps in the literal sense.
r: 1:6; 2 Kings 1:8; 6:17–29; 1 Kings 19:2; 1 Kings 19:10; Matthew 11:14; Matthew 17:12–13; Luke 1:17; John 1:21

p: Ekthambeomai is strong amazement. Some readers think Jesus' face still shone, as Moses' did.
b: The verb means "to be overwhelmed with amazement"; Mark uses it again of Jesus in Gethsemane (14:33) and of the women at the tomb (16:5–6). Why should a crowd be stunned simply to see Jesus? Some interpreters, ancient and modern, suggest a trace of the glory remained on him, as Moses' face shone when he came down from the mountain and the people were afraid (Exodus 34:29–30). Others think the crowd was simply surprised at his sudden arrival in the middle of the dispute. Mark does not explain.

a: A speechless spirit has hold of him
p: The symptoms sound like epilepsy. Mark, like his world, speaks of a spirit; readers today hold both views together or apart.
b: Falling, foaming, grinding the teeth and going stiff (9:18, 20, 26) match what is now called a seizure. Matthew 17:15 calls the boy "moonstruck," the ancient word for epilepsy. Some ancient doctors already denied that the "sacred disease" had a divine or demonic cause (the Hippocratic treatise On the Sacred Disease). Mark tells the story as the defeat of an evil spirit, as the Gospels tell all exorcisms. Christians today differ: some see a medical condition described in the language of its time, some see real spiritual oppression, some see both.

p: Jesus comes down the mountain to unbelief, as Moses came down from Sinai to the golden calf.
b: "Faithless generation" echoes Moses' song about "a crooked and twisted generation" (Deuteronomy 32:5, 20). Like Moses descending to find the people worshiping a calf (Exodus 32:15–19), Jesus comes down to disciples who could not help and scribes arguing. Who is meant? Probably everyone present: the crowd, the scribes, the father and the disciples. "How long must I endure you?" sounds like God's own complaint about Israel in the wilderness (Numbers 14:11, 27). See the note at Matthew 17:17.
r: Deuteronomy 32:5; Deuteronomy 32:20; Exodus 32:15–19; Numbers 14:11; Numbers 14:27; Matthew 17:17

a: For the one who believes, anything is possible.
p: Whose faith does Jesus mean, the father's or his own? Readers take it both ways.
b: Jesus throws the father's words back at him: "'If you are able'?" The question is not Jesus' ability but faith. Most readers take "the one who believes" to be the father: God can do anything for someone who trusts him (11:23–24). Some take it of Jesus himself, the believer through whom God acts; in Gethsemane he himself prays to his Father that everything is possible for him (14:36). Both fit Mark: all things are possible for God (10:27), and faith is the open door. The promise is not a formula; the same Gospel shows Jesus' own prayer answered with the cross.

p: The father admits faith and doubt in one breath. Christians have prayed his words ever since.
b: The father does not claim a perfect faith; he gives Jesus what he has and asks for help with the rest. His boy is healed. Mark's story honors honest, struggling trust, in contrast to the disciples, whom Jesus calls part of a faithless generation (9:19). Many preachers and writers have taken the cry as a model prayer for believers who doubt. The Byzantine text adds "with tears" and "Lord" (see the variant).

a: raised him, and he rose up
p: The boy seems dead, then Jesus "raised" him and he "rose." Mark uses the words of resurrection.
b: Mark tells this right after the disciples asked what "rising from among the dead" meant (9:10). The boy lies like a corpse, and many say he has died (9:26); Jesus takes his hand, "raised" (ēgeiren) him, and he "rose" (anestē), the two verbs used for Jesus' resurrection (14:28; 16:6; 8:31). The scene recalls Jairus' daughter, whom Jesus took by the hand and who rose (5:41–42). Mark's readers could see a small picture of the resurrection Jesus had just predicted.

a: Nothing can make this kind come out
p: Jesus did not pray aloud in the story. Prayer here seems to mean dependence on God, not a technique.
b: The disciples had been given authority over unclean spirits (6:7, 13) and had used it. Now they failed. Jesus' answer is "prayer," yet in the story he simply commands the spirit. Many interpreters conclude that Jesus means a life of prayer: power over evil is not a skill the disciples own but comes from depending on God, as Jesus himself prayed alone (1:35; 6:46). The common later addition "and fasting" (see the variant) reflects the church's practice of fasting before exorcisms and baptisms. On how churches today deal with evil spirits, see the card at Tobit 6.

a: The Son of Man is being handed over into human hands
p: Shorter and perhaps older than the first. "Handed over" may mean by Judas, by the leaders, or by God.
b: Paradidotai, "is being handed over," is in the present tense, as if it were already under way. The same verb is used for Judas' betrayal (3:19; 14:10), for the leaders' handing Jesus to Pilate (15:1) and Pilate's to the soldiers (15:15), and in the Greek of Isaiah 53:6, 12 for God's giving up of his servant. Joachim Jeremias argued that a short saying like "the man will be handed over to men" may be the oldest form of the predictions; the play between Son of Man and "human hands" works in Aramaic too.

a: they were too frightened to question him
p: Mark says the disciples did not understand and were afraid. Matthew says instead that they were deeply grieved.
b: Mark's disciples understand neither the first prediction (8:32) nor this one, and fear keeps them from asking. Matthew 17:23 has them "deeply grieved," which assumes they understood; Luke 9:45 says the meaning was hidden from them. This is a known pattern: Matthew and Luke often soften Mark's picture of the disciples. For Mark, misunderstanding and fear are honest marks of real followers, up to the women who flee the tomb "afraid" (16:8).

p: In a world built on honor and rank, the question was natural. Even the Dead Sea community sat by rank.
b: Ancient society was arranged by honor: who sat where, who spoke first, who served whom. The Community Rule from Qumran tells members to sit in order of rank, priests first, then elders, then the rest of the people, each in his place (1QS 6:8–9). Jesus has just spoken of being handed over to die, and his disciples argue about precedence. It happens again after the third prediction, when James and John ask for the best seats (10:35–45), and at the Last Supper in Luke 22:24.

a: he will be last of everyone and everyone's servant
p: Diakonos was a table servant. Jesus turns the ladder of rank upside down; 10:43–45 explains why.
b: Diakonos first meant someone who waited on tables, later a church "deacon." Jesus does not forbid wanting to be first; he redefines what first means. Jesus sat down to teach, as Jewish teachers did. He repeats the saying after the third prediction with a sharper word, "slave of all," and grounds it in his own life: the Son of Man came to serve, not to be served (10:43–45).

a: with his arms around the child
p: Children had no status in the ancient world. Only Mark says Jesus took the child in his arms.
b: A small child (paidion) was the least important person in a household, a dependent with no rights or honor; the same word could mean a young slave. The point is not that children are innocent but that they are low. Jesus places one in the middle of men arguing about rank and embraces the child, a detail only Mark gives, here and in 10:16. Welcoming such a person is welcoming Jesus, and welcoming Jesus is welcoming God.

p: The sayings in 9:37–50 are linked by repeated words: name, trip up, fire, salt.
b: From here to the end of the chapter, Mark's sayings are strung together by key words, as was common in oral teaching. "In my name" links the child (9:37), the outside exorcist (9:38–39) and the cup of water (9:41). "Trip up" links 9:42–47. "Fire" links 9:48 and 9:49, and "salt" links 9:49 and 9:50. Many scholars think Mark or his tradition gathered sayings spoken at different times this way; Matthew and Luke place some of them elsewhere (Matthew 5:13; Matthew 10:42; Matthew 18:6–9).

a: we saw a man throwing out demons in your name
t: The outsider who used Jesus' name
p: Like Joshua asking Moses to stop two men prophesying in the camp, John wants an outsider stopped.
b: In Numbers 11:26–29, two elders prophesied away from the tent of meeting, and Joshua said, "My lord Moses, hold them back!" Moses answered that he wished all the LORD's people were prophets. Jesus answers John in the same spirit. Using the names of powerful figures in exorcisms was common: a Greek magical papyrus adjures a demon "by the god of the Hebrews, Jesus" (Greek Magical Papyri IV.3019–3020), and Acts 19:13–16 tells of Jewish exorcists who tried Jesus' name. Note John's complaint: the man was not following "us." The disciples have just failed to cast out a spirit themselves (9:18). The Byzantine text and the KJV add "who does not follow us" earlier in the verse as well, so John makes the complaint twice.

t: Not against us, so for us
p: Elsewhere Jesus says, "Anyone who is not on my side is against me." The two sayings face different situations.
b: Matthew 12:30 and Luke 11:23 have the reverse: "Anyone who is not on my side is against me" (Matthew 12:30). There the subject is the struggle with Satan, where no one can be neutral. Here it is a person doing Jesus' work without joining the Twelve, and Jesus is generous. Both forms circulated as proverbs: Cicero reminds Julius Caesar that he had said he counted everyone who was not against him as his own (For Ligarius 33). Luke keeps both sayings (Luke 9:50; Luke 11:23). The Byzantine text reads "you" (see the variant).

p: The only place in Jesus' own words where Mark uses "Christ" without the article, as a name. Compare 1:1, the title.
b: Everywhere else in the story Christos has the article and means "the Messiah" (8:29; 12:35; 13:21; 14:61; 15:32); only Mark's title uses it as a name, "Jesus Christ" (1:1). Here it has none: literally "in the name that you are Christ's." Paul writes the same way: "you are Christ's" (1 Corinthians 3:23; compare Romans 8:9; 2 Corinthians 10:7). Many scholars conclude that the wording reflects the church in which Mark's Gospel was told; others think Jesus could speak of belonging to the Messiah. Matthew 10:42 has "in the name of a disciple." A cup of water was the smallest kindness, but for missionaries who depended on strangers it could be life.

t: A millstone turned by a donkey
p: Not a hand mill but the great upper stone of a mill pulled by a donkey. Drowning was a known execution.
b: Households ground flour with small hand mills, but a mylos onikos was a large mill whose upper stone was turned by a donkey; large basalt millstones of this kind have been found at Capernaum and other Galilean sites. Hung around a man's neck, it would sink him beyond rescue. Josephus says that Galileans once drowned supporters of Herod in the Sea of Galilee (Antiquities 14.450). "Trips up" is skandalizō, to make someone stumble into sin or lose faith. "These little ones who believe in me" are the child of 9:36 and any humble believer, perhaps including the outsider of 9:38.

p: Gehenna is the Valley of Hinnom by Jerusalem. The usual English "hell" hides the place name.
b: Geenna comes from the Hebrew ge hinnom, the valley south of Jerusalem where kings of Judah burned children to idols (2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31). Jeremiah said it would become the "Valley of Slaughter" (Jeremiah 7:32). Later Jewish writings made it the place of fiery judgment (1 Enoch 27:1–2). Mark's "the fire that cannot be put out" draws on Isaiah 66:24 (see 9:48). The old idea that the valley was a city rubbish dump with ever-burning fires appears first in the Middle Ages and is not attested in ancient sources. On views of final punishment, see the cards at Matthew 10:28 and Isaiah 66.
r: 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 7:31–32; Isaiah 66:24; 1 Enoch 27:1–2; Matthew 5:22; Matthew 10:28; Matthew 18:9

a: If your hand trips you up, cut it off.
p: Almost all readers take this as hyperbole: give up whatever leads to sin. A few have taken it literally.
b: Figurative: the common reading, ancient and modern: no price is too high to avoid ruin, and the hand, foot and eye stand for what we do, where we go and what we desire. Literal: Eusebius reports that the young Origen took Matthew 19:12 literally and castrated himself (Church History 6.8), and the church condemned such acts (Council of Nicaea, canon 1). Sexual sins: some scholars note a Jewish saying about cutting off a hand that touches immodestly (Mishnah Niddah 2:1) and read the hand, foot and eye as sexual. The community: some early readers took the members as people in the church who cause others to fall, compare 1 Corinthians 12.

p: Mark's word for removing the eye is ekballō, the verb he uses for throwing out demons.
b: Matthew 18:9 says "pull it out" (exelē). Mark has ekbale, "throw it out," the verb used all through his Gospel for casting out demons (1:34, 39; 3:15; 9:18, 28, 38). After a chapter about throwing out a spirit the disciples could not expel, the same word turns inward: a disciple must throw out what leads him into sin. Here Mark says "the kingdom of God" where 9:43 and 9:45 say "life": entering the kingdom and entering life are the same thing. The Byzantine text and the KJV read "the fire of Gehenna" (KJV "hell fire") at the end of the verse, as in Matthew 18:9.

a: where their worm never dies and the fire is never put out
p: Jesus applies the final verse of Isaiah, about the corpses of rebels, to Gehenna.
b: Isaiah ends with worshipers going out to look at the bodies of those who rebelled against God: "For their worm will not die, / and their fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24). Mark's Greek follows the Greek of Isaiah closely. Jewish writings applied the verse to final punishment (Judith 16:17; Sirach 7:17). Readers disagree on what the image teaches: unending conscious suffering, or a destruction that cannot be undone. The card at Isaiah 66 sets out how the churches read it.

p: One of the hardest sayings in the Gospels. It may mean judgment, purifying trial, or sacrifice.
b: Sacrifice: every offering was salted (Leviticus 2:13), and a later addition here quotes that law (see the variant): disciples are offerings to God, refined by suffering (Romans 12:1). Purifying trial: fire tests and refines, as with gold (1 Peter 1:7; 1 Peter 4:12); salt preserves. Disciples who face persecution are being made fit for God. Judgment: "everyone" may mean those thrown into Gehenna, whom fire preserves for punishment as salt preserves meat. Mark's readers in Rome, who knew believers burned under Nero (Tacitus, Annals 15.44), would hear the first two readings with special force.
r: Leviticus 2:13; Romans 12:1; 1 Peter 1:6–7; 1 Peter 4:12; Malachi 3:2–3; 1 Corinthians 3:13–15

p: Pure salt cannot lose its taste, but ancient salt often came mixed with other minerals that remained when the salt leached out.
b: Much salt in Judea came from the Dead Sea area, crusted with gypsum and other minerals. Damp could wash out the real salt and leave a tasteless residue that looked the same. Matthew 5:13 has the saying in the Sermon on the Mount, where Jesus' followers are "the salt of the earth"; Luke 14:34–35 places it after the cost of discipleship. Mark's form is the most compact.

a: Keep salt in yourselves, and keep peace with one another.
p: Salt sealed covenants and was shared at meals. The chapter that began with a quarrel ends with a call to peace.
b: In Israel salt stood for a lasting covenant: "Do not leave the salt of your God's covenant out of your grain offering" (Leviticus 2:13), and Numbers 18:19 speaks of "a covenant of salt for all time." To "eat someone's salt" meant to share his table and owe him loyalty (Ezra 4:14). Salt also stood for wise speech (Colossians 4:6). The disciples began this section arguing over who ranked highest (9:34) and trying to stop an outsider (9:38); Jesus ends by telling them to keep what makes them a covenant people and to live at peace.
r: Leviticus 2:13; Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5; Ezra 4:14; Colossians 4:6; Romans 12:18; 9:34
